legions.name: Legio VII (Caesar's Seventh)
legions.endNote: veterans settled at Baeterrae? and Luca; legion reconstituted by Octavian, ancestor of VII Claudia

stations.base: River Sabis (Sambre), battle with the Nervii
stations.note: held the right wing against the Nervii with XII

legions.summary: One of the four veteran legions Caesar inherited in Gallia Cisalpina in 58 BC (VII-X), probably raised by Pompey in Spain in the 60s. It fought at every major engagement of the Gallic War, including both crossings to Britain, then for Caesar at Ilerda, Pharsalus and Thapsus.
legions.detail: In 57 BC on the Sabis the VII and XII were so compressed by the Nervian assault that the standards were bunched and almost every centurion of XII's fourth cohort fell before Caesar himself went to the front line (BG 2.25-26). In Britain in 55 BC the Seventh was ambushed while foraging and rescued by Caesar (BG 4.32). Discharged veterans were settled in colonies (Baeterrae is 'Septimanorum'); the legion was re-formed by Octavian and became VII Macedonica, later VII Claudia.

legions.name: Legio VIII (Caesar's Eighth)
legions.endNote: veterans settled at Forum Iulii (colonia Octavanorum); reconstituted, ancestor of VIII Augusta

stations.note: joined with the IX on the left wing because both were understrength

legions.summary: Veteran legion of Caesar's Gallic army, probably of Pompeian Spanish origin like VII and IX. It was at Gergovia, Alesia, the Dyrrachium lines, Pharsalus and Thapsus, and its veterans were settled in Italy and at Forum Iulii.
legions.detail: At Pharsalus the Eighth was so depleted that Caesar paired it with the Ninth to form a single line unit (BC 3.89). The legion re-formed after 44 BC took the name Augusta, a sign of a re-raising or of a battle honour under Octavian.

legions.name: Legio IX (Caesar's Ninth)
legions.endNote: disbanded after Thapsus, veterans settled in Picenum; re-formed by Octavian (later IX Hispana)

stations.base: River Sabis (Sambre), battle with the Nervii

legions.summary: The Ninth served through the Gallic War and the civil war. Its mutiny at Placentia in 49 BC, when Caesar threatened decimation and executed twelve ringleaders, is one of the classic episodes of late Republican army discipline.
legions.detail: Appian (BC 2.47) and Dio (41.26-35) describe the Placentia mutiny over delayed pay and booty; Caesar's own Bellum Civile passes over it in silence. The legion lost heavily at Dyrrachium in 48 BC (BC 3.45-46). After Thapsus its veterans were settled in Picenum; Octavian raised a new IX that served against Sextus Pompey ('Triumphalis'?) and in the Cantabrian war.
legions.debate: Whether the imperial IX Hispana descends directly from Caesar's Ninth or is a fresh Octavianic creation is disputed.

legions.name: Legio X Equestris
legions.endNote: veterans settled at Narbo (45 BC); re-formed, later merged into X Gemina

stations.note: Caesar mounts its men on Gallic horses to meet Ariovistus

stations.base: River Sabis (Sambre), battle with the Nervii

stations.note: its aquilifer leaps first into the surf
decided the battle on the right

legions.summary: Caesar's favourite legion, raised by him as governor of Hispania Ulterior (61 BC). Its nickname 'Equestris' comes from 58 BC, when Caesar mounted its men on Gallic cavalry horses to escort him to Ariovistus and a soldier quipped that he was making them knights.
legions.detail: The standard-bearer of the X led the jump into the sea off Kent in 55 BC (BG 4.25). In 47 BC the legion mutinied in Campania and marched on Rome; Caesar ended it by addressing the men as 'Quirites' (civilians) rather than 'commilitones' (Suet. Iul. 70; App. BC 2.93). It fought at Thapsus and decided Munda, then its veterans were settled at Narbo. A re-formed X fought for Lepidus and Antony; merged with another legion under Augustus, it became X Gemina.

legions.name: Legio I Germanica
legions.endNote: surrendered to the Gallic empire of Classicus in the Batavian revolt; disbanded by Vespasian, men drafted into VII Gemina

stations.note: probably the legion stripped of the title Augusta by Agrippa in 19 BC

legions.summary: Lower Rhine legion that started the mutiny of AD 14 at Ara Ubiorum and twelve years later the proclamation of Vitellius. It ended in disgrace: after swearing allegiance to the Imperium Galliarum in 70 it was dissolved.
legions.detail: Agrippa took away the honorific Augusta from a legion after its poor performance against the Cantabri in 19 BC (Dio 54.11.5); I Germanica is the usual candidate. Under Germanicus it took part in the campaigns of AD 14-16. On 2 January 69 its legate Fabius Valens hailed Vitellius at Colonia, and a strong detachment marched to Italy and fought at Bedriacum. Besieged at Bonna and later at Novaesium by Civilis, the remnant with XVI Gallica took the oath to the Gallic empire, was paraded to Trier in humiliation (Tac. Hist. 4.62), and was disbanded. Its survivors helped form VII Gemina.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Adiutrix
legions.endNote: listed at Brigetio in the Notitia Dignitatum

stations.note: Dacia during and after Trajan's wars

legions.summary: Raised from the marines of the Misenum fleet late in Nero's reign and given legionary standards by Galba (diploma of 22 December 68). After service on the Rhine it became the long-term garrison of Brigetio on the Pannonian Danube from Hadrian's time.
legions.detail: Galba's entry into Rome in October 68 was marked by the slaughter of marines who demanded an eagle at the Milvian Bridge (Tac. Hist. 1.6; Suet. Galba 12); the survivors became I Adiutrix. It fought for Otho at the first battle of Bedriacum and broke XXI Rapax's front line (Tac. Hist. 2.43). Brigetio was its base for three centuries; the legion styled itself pia fidelis bis and later Constans. A Hadrianic-period tile and stamp series documents its building activity throughout Pannonia.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Italica
legions.endNote: listed in the Notitia at Novae and Sexaginta Prista

stations.note: stationed at Lugdunum on its way to the East
Vitellian army at both battles of Bedriacum

legions.summary: Raised by Nero in 66 for a planned expedition to the Caspian Gates, its recruits all Italians six Roman feet tall, nicknamed 'the phalanx of Alexander the Great' (Suet. Nero 19.2). From 70 it garrisoned Novae on the Lower Danube for more than three centuries.
legions.detail: Stationed at Lugdunum in 68-69, it sided with Vitellius and fought at both battles of Bedriacum. At Novae Polish-Bulgarian excavations have uncovered its principia, a large valetudinarium and a late-antique episcopal complex built over the fortress. Vexillations served in Mauretania (Antonine period) and in the Crimea at Charax.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Minervia
legions.endNote: last attested in the early 4th century at Bonna
legions.summary: Raised by Domitian in 82/83 for his war against the Chatti and named after his patron goddess Minerva. It stayed at Bonna throughout its existence and won the titles pia fidelis for remaining loyal during Saturninus's revolt at Mainz in 89.
legions.detail: Hadrian commanded I Minervia during Trajan's second Dacian war (105-106) (HA Hadr. 3.6). Vexillations fought in Lucius Verus's Parthian war and the Marcomannic wars, and the legion supported Septimius Severus against Clodius Albinus in 197. It struck coins as a Gallic empire unit under Victorinus (269-271).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Parthica
legions.endNote: in the Notitia at Constantina (Tella) as Prima Parthica Nisibena

stations.note: Singara captured by Shapur II in 360 and the garrison deported

legions.summary: One of three Parthian legions (I-III) raised by Septimius Severus for his eastern campaigns of 195-198, and the garrison of the new province of Mesopotamia at Singara under the Jebel Sinjar.
legions.detail: Unlike the senatorial legions, the Parthian legions were commanded by equestrian prefects. Singara fell to Shapur II in 360 after a siege in which the two legions inside (I Parthica and I Flavia) were captured (Amm. 20.6.8). The successor unit sat at Constantina after Jovian surrendered Nisibis and Singara in 363.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio I Macriana Liberatrix
legions.endNote: disbanded by Galba after Macer's execution

stations.note: raised in Africa beside III Augusta

legions.summary: Short-lived legion raised in spring 68 by the legate of III Augusta, L. Clodius Macer, who revolted against Nero, struck denarii with the legend LEG I LIB MACRIANA, and threatened Rome's grain supply. Galba had Macer killed and dissolved the legion.

legions.name: Legio II Augusta
legions.endNote: listed at Rutupiae (Richborough) under the comes litoris Saxonici

stations.note: Cantabrian war; veterans settled at Emerita? and Caesaraugusta
built the first legionary fortress at Strasbourg

stations.base: Midlands of Britain (series of campaign bases)
stations.note: Vespasian's campaign in the south-west: 30 battles, 20 oppida, the Isle of Wight (Suet. Vesp. 4)

legions.summary: The Second Augusta invaded Britain in 43 under the future emperor Vespasian and spent more than two centuries at Isca (Caerleon), building large stretches of Hadrian's and the Antonine Walls. Its camp prefect Poenius Postumus refused to join Suetonius Paulinus against Boudica and fell on his sword after the victory (Tac. Ann. 14.37).
legions.detail: Under Vespasian the legion conquered the Durotriges: the war cemetery and ballista bolt in a spine at Maiden Castle are often linked to its assault. Exeter's fortress (c. 55-75) was followed by Caerleon, where the amphitheatre, baths and barracks are the best preserved of any British fortress. Building stones name it on both northern walls. By the late 3rd century part of it held the Saxon Shore fort at Richborough, where the Notitia places it.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Manning, The Fortress Excavations at Caerleon

legions.name: Legio II Adiutrix
legions.endNote: listed at Aquincum in the Notitia
legions.summary: Raised by Vespasian from the marines of the Ravenna fleet (constituted 7 March 70), it served in Britain under Cerialis and Agricola before being pulled out to the Danube after Domitian's Dacian setbacks. From the late 1st century it was the garrison of Aquincum, the capital of Pannonia Inferior.
legions.detail: Its withdrawal from Deva c. 87 forced the abandonment of the newly built fortress at Inchtuthil and of Agricola's Scottish conquests: Tacitus' bitter 'perdomita Britannia et statim omissa' (Hist. 1.2). Hadrian served as one of its tribunes (c. 95). At Aquincum its fortress lies under modern Óbuda, with a large amphitheatre for the garrison.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio II Italica
legions.endNote: listed at Lauriacum and Lentia in the Notitia
legions.summary: Raised with III Italica by Marcus Aurelius in 165-166, from Italian recruits, as the Marcomannic crisis loomed. It became the first legion permanently based in Noricum, whose governor was now its legate.
legions.detail: The new legion's arrival upgraded Noricum to a praetorian province. Lauriacum (Enns) became one of the largest fortresses on the Danube and a late-antique bishopric; the Life of Severinus describes its last Roman garrison and refugees in the 470s-480s.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio II Parthica
legions.endNote: captured at Bezabde by Shapur II (Amm. 20.7.1)

stations.note: first legion permanently stationed in Italy; campaigns in the east under Caracalla, Severus Alexander, Gordian III

legions.summary: Severus's Second Parthian was garrisoned at Castra Albana, 20 km from Rome, a political revolution: a legion in Italy as the emperor's strategic reserve. It took part in nearly every 3rd-century imperial campaign in the East.
legions.detail: Its men were involved in the murder of Caracalla near Carrhae in 217 and then backed Elagabalus against Macrinus at Raphanea/Immae in 218. It acclaimed Maximinus Thrax in 235 and in 238 its men murdered him outside Aquileia. Tombstones at Apamea in Syria record its winter quarters there in 215-218 and 231-233. A detachment served at Bezabde on the Tigris, which Shapur II stormed in 360.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Balty, 'Apamea in Syria in the second and third centuries AD', JRS 78 (1988)

legions.name: Legio II Traiana Fortis
legions.endNote: listed at Parembole (Upper Egypt) and Apollonopolis in the Notitia

stations.note: single legion of Egypt after XXII Deiotariana vanished

legions.summary: Raised by Trajan for the Dacian or Parthian wars, II Traiana became the legion of Egypt at Nicopolis outside Alexandria from Hadrian's reign, alone after XXII Deiotariana disappeared.
legions.detail: It sent vexillations to Judaea during the Bar Kokhba war (132-135). From Severus onwards it bore the name Germanica after Caracalla's Alemannic campaign of 213. Egyptian papyri preserve an unusually rich record of its recruits, pay and discharge procedure.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio III Augusta
legions.endNote: disbanded 238 by Gordian III, restored 253; Tertio Augustani among the African comitatenses in the Notitia

stations.note: Hadrian's address to the army of Africa in 128 inscribed on the parade ground column

legions.summary: The single legion of Roman Africa, based successively at Ammaedara, Theveste and Lambaesis, it built roads, aqueducts and towns such as Thamugadi across Numidia. Gordian III dissolved it in 238 because its legate Capelianus had destroyed Gordian I and II at Carthage.
legions.detail: Under Tiberius it fought the seven-year guerrilla war of Tacfarinas (17-24). Its legate was the only commander of a legion in a senatorial province until Caligula transferred control from the proconsul. Hadrian's adlocutio at Lambaesis (CIL VIII 18042, July 128) is the fullest surviving text of an emperor addressing troops, praising manoeuvres and criticising details. Its name was erased from inscriptions in 238 (damnatio) and recut after 253.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Le Bohec, La Troisième Légion Auguste (1989)

legions.name: Legio III Cyrenaica
legions.endNote: listed at Bostra in the Notitia

stations.note: Arabia after the annexation of Nabataea; possibly only from c. 123

legions.summary: Probably raised by Antony or Lepidus with its name from Cyrenaica, III Cyrenaica was part of the Augustan garrison of Egypt. After Trajan annexed Nabataea in 106 it became the legion of Arabia at Bostra, where it stayed into the 5th century.
legions.detail: It took part in Aelius Gallus's expedition into Arabia Felix (26-25 BC) or Petronius's war with Meroe (24-22 BC). A vexillation besieged Jerusalem with Titus in 70. Papyri from Bostra (the letters of Apollinarius, 107) describe the new province: 'while others are breaking stones all day long, I am a principalis and do nothing' (P. Mich. VIII 466).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Bowersock, Roman Arabia (1983)

legions.name: Legio III Gallica
legions.endNote: in the Notitia at Danaba (Phoenice), location not securely identified

stations.note: Syrian garrison, base probably at Raphanea
Moesia; destroyed a Rhoxolani raid in winter 68/69
restored by Severus Alexander; later at Danaba

legions.summary: A Caesarian legion of Gallic recruits that spent most of its life in Syria. At the second battle of Bedriacum (October 69) its soldiers, used to Syrian custom, saluted the rising sun, which the Vitellians took as the arrival of eastern reinforcements (Tac. Hist. 3.24-25).
legions.detail: It fought with Antony in Media Atropatene (36 BC) and with Corbulo in Armenia (58-63). Transferred to Moesia in 68, it was the first Danubian legion to declare for Vespasian. In 218-219 its legate Verus tried to make himself emperor and Elagabalus dissolved the legion (Dio 80.7.1); Severus Alexander re-formed it.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio III Italica
legions.endNote: listed in Raetia (Castra Regina and detachments along the Danube-Iller line) in the Notitia

stations.note: Raetia before the fortress was finished
building inscription of the gate dated 179

legions.summary: Twin of II Italica, raised in 165-166 and sent to Raetia, whose governor became a senatorial legate. Its fortress at Regensburg is dated precisely by the inscription from the Porta Praetoria (CIL III 11965) to 179.
legions.detail: The Regensburg fortress gate (Porta Praetoria) still stands partly in the city. In the late empire the legion was split into detachments along the Danube and the Iller, as the Notitia shows (Not. Occ. 35).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio III Parthica
legions.endNote: in the Notitia at Apatna in Osrhoene (site uncertain)

stations.note: Mesopotamia/Osroene; Rhesaena coins with the legion's emblem

legions.summary: Third of Severus's Parthian legions, garrisoned in Osroene/Mesopotamia, probably at Rhesaena (Ras al-Ayn) where coins of the colonia carry its vexillum.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio IV Macedonica
legions.endNote: disbanded after the Batavian revolt; reconstituted as IV Flavia Felix

stations.note: Hispania Tarraconensis; tile stamps at Herrera de Pisuerga

legions.summary: Raised by Caesar in 48 BC, at Mutina for Octavian in 43, and then for seven decades the garrison of Pisoraca in northern Spain. Moved to Mainz under Claudius, it joined XXII Primigenia in throwing down Galba's images on 1 January 69, the act that launched Vitellius's bid.
legions.detail: In 70 the legion joined Civilis and Classicus' Imperium Galliarum; Vespasian dissolved it and re-raised it as IV Flavia Felix. The rejection of Galba at Mainz is told in Tacitus Hist. 1.55-56.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio IV Flavia Felix
legions.endNote: listed at Singidunum in the Notitia

stations.note: garrison of the new province of Dacia

legions.summary: Re-formed by Vespasian from the dissolved IV Macedonica, it held Burnum in Dalmatia, then Berzobis in Dacia, and from Hadrian's reign Singidunum (Belgrade), its base for three centuries.
legions.detail: Its lion emblem echoes Flavian iconography. The fortress of Singidunum lies under Belgrade's Kalemegdan citadel. Vexillations fought in the Marcomannic wars and in Severus Alexander's Persian war.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio IV Scythica
legions.endNote: in the Notitia at Oresa (Strata Diocletiana)

stations.note: title from M. Licinius Crassus's campaign against Bastarnae and Getae (29-28 BC)
with Corbulo; capitulated with XII Fulminata at Rhandeia (62)
tile stamps confirm the fortress at the Euphrates crossing

legions.summary: Probably an Antonian legion that took its title from victories over 'Scythians' on the Lower Danube. In 62 it was humiliated with XII Fulminata at Rhandeia under Caesennius Paetus, then held the Euphrates crossing at Zeugma for two centuries.
legions.detail: The Rhandeia capitulation (Tac. Ann. 15.7-17) obliged the Roman army to build a bridge for the Parthians and leave Armenia. At Zeugma, rescue excavations before the Birecik dam flooded the city (2000) recovered a large deposit of clay sealings and military material.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio V Alaudae
legions.endNote: destroyed in Domitian's Dacian wars (86, possibly 92)

stations.note: stood against Juba's elephants, hence its emblem
lost its eagle in the clades Lolliana of 16 BC
with XXI Rapax, later XV Primigenia

legions.summary: Caesar's legion of Transalpine Gauls, raised at his own expense in 52 BC and later given citizenship en bloc: the first legion of non-citizens. The 'Larks' (alaudae, from the crested helmets) took the elephant as emblem after facing Juba's elephants at Thapsus.
legions.detail: It fought at Munda and Philippi, then in Spain and on the Rhine. Its eagle was lost when M. Lollius was defeated by the Sugambri in 16 BC (Vell. 2.97). At Vetera it mutinied in AD 14. Most of it marched with Vitellius in 69 and fought on at Cremona; the rump at Vetera was besieged by Civilis. Sent to Moesia by Vespasian, it vanishes in Domitian's Dacian wars, most likely with Cornelius Fuscus in 86.
legions.debate: Whether the legion lost with Fuscus in 86 was V Alaudae, and whether the legion lost 'with its legate' against the Sarmatians in 92 (Suet. Dom. 6) was XXI Rapax, is argued from absence of later evidence.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Syme, 'Rhine and Danube legions under Domitian', JRS 18 (1928)

legions.name: Legio V Macedonica
legions.endNote: listed at Oescus and Variniana in the Notitia; later a comitatensis unit in Egypt

stations.note: Armenia with Corbulo, then the Jewish war under Vespasian; camp at Emmaus
returned after the evacuation of Dacia

legions.summary: An Augustan legion of the Balkan army that served six centuries in Moesia, Judaea and Dacia. Its tour from Oescus to Troesmis to Potaissa and back to Oescus traces the advance and retreat of the Danubian frontier.
legions.detail: Under Vespasian it besieged Gamala and Jerusalem; tombstones of its soldiers survive at Emmaus. At Potaissa (Turda) it defended Dacia against the Marcomanni and Costoboci, winning the titles pia constans and, under Gallienus, VII pia VII fidelis. After 271 it returned to Oescus, then part of it went to Egypt (Memphis) in the Notitia.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio VI Ferrata
legions.endNote: disappears from the record in the late 3rd century

stations.note: Syrian garrison; with Corbulo in Armenia
possibly the first garrison of Arabia

legions.summary: Caesar's 'Ironclad' Sixth fought at Pharsalus and Zela, served Antony and then garrisoned Syria. From the 120s it held Caparcotna in Galilee; the place-name Legio survives in Arabic Lajjun beside Megiddo.
legions.detail: It defeated the Parthians in Corbulo's campaigns and in 69 its veterans marched with Mucianus to secure Italy for Vespasian. A diploma and building inscriptions place it in Judaea during the Bar Kokhba war. At Lajjun, excavations since 2013 have located its fortress and principia.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Tepper, Adams & David, 'The Roman legionary base at Legio' (2016)

legions.name: Legio VI Victrix
legions.endNote: listed at Eboracum under the dux Britanniarum

stations.note: Tarraconensis garrison; Galba proclaimed with it in 68

stations.base: Vetera II (Xanten, eroded by the Rhine)

stations.note: came to Britain with Hadrian's governor Platorius Nepos

legions.summary: Octavian's Sixth served a century in Spain, where it backed Galba's revolt in 68, then on the Lower Rhine, and from 122 at York, where it helped build Hadrian's Wall and stayed for almost three centuries.
legions.detail: At York, Septimius Severus died in 211 and Constantius I in 306, with Constantine proclaimed emperor by the troops there. The legion is the last legion in Britain recorded in the Notitia, under the dux Britanniarum.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)

legions.name: Legio VII Claudia
legions.endNote: listed at Viminacium in the Notitia
legions.summary: Descendant of Caesar's VII, the legion won the title Claudia pia fidelis by refusing to join the revolt of Camillus Scribonianus in Dalmatia in 42. It held Viminacium, the capital of Moesia Superior, for nearly four centuries.
legions.detail: Claudius awarded the honorific to VII and XI after their loyalty in 42 (Dio 60.15.4). At Viminacium the fortress, cemeteries (over 13,000 graves excavated) and an amphitheatre have been excavated in rescue work near the Kostolac power station.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio VII Gemina
legions.endNote: listed at Legio (León) in the Notitia

stations.note: second battle of Bedriacum for Vespasian
Rhine after the Batavian revolt; merged with survivors of I Germanica

legions.summary: Raised in Spain by Galba in 68 as VII Galbiana, re-formed as VII Gemina in 70 by merger with survivors of I Germanica. From 74 it was the sole legion of Spain, and its fortress gave León its name.
legions.detail: At the second battle of Bedriacum its senior centurions died defending the eagle (Tac. Hist. 3.22). At León it supervised the gold mines of Asturia and Gallaecia (Las Médulas). Trajan, born at Italica, was its legate c. 89 and marched it to the Rhine against Saturninus.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio VIII Augusta
legions.endNote: listed among the comitatenses as Octavani

stations.note: vexillation fortress during the Batavian aftermath

legions.summary: Caesar's Eighth, re-formed after Actium, served in Pannonia and Moesia before the Flavians brought it to Upper Germany. From about 90 it was the garrison of Strasbourg for more than three centuries.
legions.detail: It took part in the Pannonian mutiny of AD 14 at Poetovio. Under Claudius it helped annex Thrace (46). In 69 it marched for Vespasian. At Mirebeau a vexillation fortress with tiles stamped by detachments of several legions has been excavated.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio IX Hispana
legions.endNote: last securely dated at York in 107/108; vanishes before c. 165

stations.note: Pannonia; vexillation against Tacfarinas in Africa 20-24
vexillation fortress; Cerialis's column cut up by Boudica
tile stamps and a pendant at Nijmegen

legions.summary: The famous 'lost legion'. IX Hispana invaded Britain in 43, was mauled by Boudica in 60/61, founded the fortress at York in 71, and then disappears after an inscription of 107/108.
legions.detail: Petillius Cerialis led part of the IX to relieve Camulodunum in 61 and lost most of its infantry (Tac. Ann. 14.32). The legion fought at Mons Graupius country under Agricola, and a night attack on its camp in 82 nearly destroyed it (Agr. 26). The York gate inscription of Trajan's 12th tribunician year is the last dated record in Britain. It is absent from the list of legions on the columna in Rome (CIL VI 3492, c. 165).
legions.debate: Three positions. (1) Destroyed in northern Britain c. 117-120, when Hadrian's biographer says the Britons 'could not be held under Roman control' (HA Hadr. 5.2) and Fronto alludes to heavy losses in Britain; the Victorian thesis behind Rosemary Sutcliff's Eagle of the Ninth. (2) Transferred to Nijmegen (stamped tiles, a silver-plated pendant, careers of officers such as L. Aemilius Karus whose tribunate seems to postdate 120) and destroyed later, either in the Bar Kokhba war (132-135) or at Elegeia in Armenia in 161 when Severianus's legion was annihilated (Dio 71.2.1). (3) Disbanded. The Nijmegen material is often dated to c. 104-120 by vexillations rather than the whole legion, so the debate is open (Birley; Keppie; Campbell, 'The Fate of the Ninth', 2018).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Keppie, 'The fate of the Ninth Legion: a problem for the eastern provinces?' (1989)
Campbell, The Fate of the Ninth (2018)

legions.name: Legio X Fretensis
legions.endNote: listed at Aila in the Notitia

stations.note: Jewish war: winter camp at Jericho, then the Mount of Olives siege camp at Jerusalem
siege of Masada under Flavius Silva

legions.summary: Raised by Octavian in 41/40 BC, its name records the naval war in the Straits of Messina against Sextus Pompey (Fretum Siculum). It destroyed Jerusalem in 70, besieged Masada in 73/74 and then held Jerusalem for more than two centuries before moving to Aila on the Red Sea.
legions.detail: Its siege works at Masada, including the eight camps and the great ramp, are the best preserved Roman siege system anywhere. Coins of Aelia Capitolina and tile stamps (LXF, with boar and ship) mark its presence in Jerusalem; the boar on its standard was later read by Christian and Jewish writers as a deliberate insult. Eusebius notes its transfer to Aila (Onomasticon 6.17-20).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Richmond, 'The Roman siege-works of Masàda', JRS 52 (1962)

legions.name: Legio X Gemina
legions.endNote: listed at Vindobona in the Notitia
legions.summary: Heir of Caesar's Tenth Equestris, re-formed as Gemina by merging two legions after Actium. After a century in Spain and three decades at Nijmegen it settled at Vindobona, the origin of modern Vienna, where Marcus Aurelius may have died in 180.
legions.detail: Veterans of X Gemina and V Alaudae founded Emerita Augusta (Mérida) in 25 BC. At Nijmegen it rebuilt the Hunerberg fortress in stone. At Vindobona its fortress under Vienna's Innere Stadt was its home until the 5th century.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XI Claudia
legions.endNote: listed at Durostorum in the Notitia
legions.summary: Octavianic legion that, with VII, won the title Claudia pia fidelis for loyalty during the revolt of Scribonianus in 42. Burnum, Vindonissa and then Durostorum on the Lower Danube were its bases.
legions.detail: Its Neptune emblem may recall service at Actium. At Durostorum (Silistra) it was the core of Moesia Inferior's eastern defence; the city later produced the general Aetius.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XII Fulminata
legions.endNote: listed at Melitene in the Notitia

stations.note: probably the third Augustan legion of Egypt

legions.summary: The 'Thunderbolt' legion, defeated twice under bad commanders (Rhandeia 62, Beth Horon 66, where it lost its eagle) before settling at Melitene on the upper Euphrates for four centuries.
legions.detail: In the 'Rain Miracle' against the Quadi (c. 172), Dio attributes the storm to an Egyptian magician; the Christian tradition (Apollinaris of Hierapolis, Tertullian, Eusebius HE 5.5) credits the prayers of Christian soldiers of the Melitene legion and claims the name Fulminata dates from then, which is false since it is attested under Augustus. Forty soldiers of the legion are said to have been martyred at Sebaste in 320 (the Forty Martyrs).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XIII Gemina
legions.endNote: listed at Ratiaria/Aegeta (Dacia Ripensis) and at Babylon in Egypt in the Notitia
legions.summary: Heir to the legion with which Caesar crossed the Rubicon in January 49 BC. Re-formed as Gemina by Octavian, it was for 165 years the core of Roman Dacia at Apulum (Alba Iulia).
legions.detail: It fought for Otho at the first battle of Bedriacum and was humiliatingly set to build amphitheatres at Cremona and Bononia by the victors (Tac. Hist. 2.67). At Apulum its fortress became the seat of the consular governor of the Three Dacias. After Aurelian's withdrawal (c. 271-275) it moved to the new Dacia south of the Danube.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XIV Gemina Martia Victrix
legions.endNote: listed at Carnuntum in the Notitia

stations.base: Midlands of Britain (series of campaign bases)
stations.note: invasion and advance into the Midlands
withdrawn by Nero; fought for Otho

legions.summary: The legion that destroyed Boudica's host in 60/61 with part of XX, winning Nero's title Martia Victrix. Later it held Carnuntum, the capital of Pannonia Superior, where Septimius Severus was proclaimed emperor in 193.
legions.detail: Tacitus calls it 'the conquerors of Britain' (Hist. 2.11). It was with Paulinus's raid on Anglesey (60) before the revolt. In 69 it backed Otho and was sent back to Britain by Vitellius. At Carnuntum the imperial conference of 308 (Diocletian, Galerius, Maximian) met to settle the succession.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XV Apollinaris
legions.endNote: listed at Satala in the Notitia

stations.note: Corbulo, then Titus's legion in the Jewish war: Jotapata, Gamala, Jerusalem

legions.summary: Named after Apollo, Octavian's patron, it built the first fortress at Carnuntum, served under Titus at Jerusalem and from Trajan's time guarded the Armenian frontier at Satala.
legions.detail: Arrian's Order of Battle against the Alans (Ektaxis, c. 135) puts XV Apollinaris at the head of the Cappadocian army with XII Fulminata. Titus led it in Judaea while his father commanded the war; it was at the sieges of Jotapata, Gamala and Jerusalem.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XV Primigenia
legions.endNote: destroyed after the surrender of Vetera in March 70
legions.summary: Raised by Caligula in 39 for his German and British expeditions, named for Fortuna Primigenia. It perished in the Batavian revolt: after a winter siege at Vetera the starving garrison surrendered and was massacred on the march.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XVI Gallica
legions.endNote: surrendered to Classicus; disbanded and re-formed as XVI Flavia Firma
legions.summary: Augustan legion of the Rhine army that swore allegiance to the Imperium Galliarum at Novaesium in 70 after its legate Vocula was murdered, and was dissolved by Vespasian.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XVI Flavia Firma
legions.endNote: listed at Sura on the Euphrates in the Notitia
legions.summary: Vespasian re-raised the disgraced XVI Gallica as Flavia Firma ('steadfast') and sent it to the newly organised Cappadocian frontier at Satala. From Hadrian's reign it held Samosata, later Sura on the Euphrates.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XVII
legions.endNote: destroyed with Varus in the Teutoburg Forest, September AD 9; number never reused
legions.summary: One of the three legions annihilated with P. Quinctilius Varus in AD 9. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again, a unique case of numbers left vacant as ill-omened. No base known; perhaps on the Lower Rhine or the Lippe.
legions.detail: The eagles were recovered piecemeal: one by L. Stertinius among the Bructeri in 15 (Tac. Ann. 1.60), one from the Marsi in 16 (Ann. 2.25), the third by P. Gabinius from the Chauci in 41 (Dio 60.8.7). The battlefield at Kalkriese, identified in 1987 by Tony Clunn's coin finds, has yielded a turf rampart, equipment and the iron face mask of a cavalry helmet.
scholarship: Wells, The Battle That Stopped Rome (2003)
Rost & Wilbers-Rost, Kalkriese reports

legions.name: Legio XVIII
legions.endNote: destroyed with Varus in the Teutoburg Forest, September AD 9; number never reused
legions.summary: One of the three legions annihilated with P. Quinctilius Varus in AD 9. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again, a unique case of numbers left vacant as ill-omened. Centurion M. Caelius's cenotaph at Vetera names it.
legions.detail: The eagles were recovered piecemeal: one by L. Stertinius among the Bructeri in 15 (Tac. Ann. 1.60), one from the Marsi in 16 (Ann. 2.25), the third by P. Gabinius from the Chauci in 41 (Dio 60.8.7). The battlefield at Kalkriese, identified in 1987 by Tony Clunn's coin finds, has yielded a turf rampart, equipment and the iron face mask of a cavalry helmet.
scholarship: Wells, The Battle That Stopped Rome (2003)
Rost & Wilbers-Rost, Kalkriese reports

legions.name: Legio XIX
legions.endNote: destroyed with Varus in the Teutoburg Forest, September AD 9; number never reused

stations.base: Dangstetten (Augustan camp on the Upper Rhine)

legions.summary: One of the three legions annihilated with P. Quinctilius Varus in AD 9. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again, a unique case of numbers left vacant as ill-omened. Lead ingots stamped L XIX from Dangstetten and Haltern.
legions.detail: The eagles were recovered piecemeal: one by L. Stertinius among the Bructeri in 15 (Tac. Ann. 1.60), one from the Marsi in 16 (Ann. 2.25), the third by P. Gabinius from the Chauci in 41 (Dio 60.8.7). The battlefield at Kalkriese, identified in 1987 by Tony Clunn's coin finds, has yielded a turf rampart, equipment and the iron face mask of a cavalry helmet.
scholarship: Wells, The Battle That Stopped Rome (2003)

legions.name: Legio XX Valeria Victrix
legions.endNote: last attested on coins of Carausius (c. 287-293)

stations.note: Great Illyrian revolt under Valerius Messallinus

legions.summary: Possibly named after M. Valerius Messallinus, under whom it distinguished itself in the Illyrian revolt of AD 6-9, the Twentieth came to Britain in 43 and for two centuries held Chester. Its title Victrix probably dates from the defeat of Boudica.
legions.detail: Agricola commanded it in 70-73. Inchtuthil, on the Tay, was a 21-hectare fortress abandoned before completion c. 86/87; the garrison buried a million iron nails (about 10 tonnes) to keep them from the Caledonians. At Chester the elliptical building inside the fortress has been interpreted as intended for a governor's palace.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XXI Rapax
legions.endNote: probably the legion destroyed with its legate by the Sarmatians in 92 (Suet. Dom. 6)

stations.note: massacred the Helvetii at Aquae Helveticae in 69

legions.summary: 'The Predator', an Augustan legion of the Rhine, notorious for brutality: in 69 it plundered Aquae Helveticae (Baden) and slaughtered the Helvetii who opposed Vitellius (Tac. Hist. 1.67). After joining Saturninus's revolt at Mainz in 89 it was sent to Pannonia and disappears.
legions.debate: Most scholars identify it with the legion lost with its legate to the Sarmatian Iazyges in 92; V Alaudae is the alternative candidate.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Syme, JRS 18 (1928)

legions.name: Legio XXII Deiotariana
legions.endNote: last attested c. 119; absent from the columna list c. 165

stations.note: Deiotarus's legions drilled in the Roman manner

legions.summary: Born as the Roman-style army of King Deiotarus of Galatia, defeated by Pharnaces at Nicopolis in 48 BC, it was taken into the Roman army when Galatia was annexed in 25 BC and posted to Egypt. It vanishes in Hadrian's reign.
legions.detail: It fought the Alexandrian Jewish riots of 66 and sent a vexillation to Titus in 70. It is last attested around 119.
legions.debate: Its end is unknown: destroyed in the Bar Kokhba war (132-135, based on the inscription of a vexillation at Jerusalem? and a late Talmudic tale of poisoned soldiers, both weak), lost in the Diaspora revolt of 115-117 in Egypt, or disbanded. It is missing from the list of c. 165 (CIL VI 3492).
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
Keppie, 'The history and disappearance of the legion XXII Deiotariana' (1990)

legions.name: Legio XXII Primigenia
legions.endNote: last attested in the 4th century at Mogontiacum

stations.base: Vetera II (Xanten, eroded by the Rhine)

legions.summary: Caligula's legion, raised in 39 for his German campaign, which threw down Galba's statues at Mainz on 1 January 69 and acclaimed Vitellius. Its loyalty to Domitian during Saturninus's revolt (89) won it pia fidelis and a return to Mainz, its home for three centuries.
legions.detail: The Jupiter Column of Mainz (AD 58/59) and the large number of its tombstones make XXII Primigenia one of the best documented legions. It built much of the Upper German limes in the Antonine period; its stamped tiles are found at forts from the Taunus to the Odenwald.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)

legions.name: Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix
legions.endNote: last attested in the 4th century at Vetera/Colonia Ulpia Traiana

stations.base: Vetera II (Xanten, eroded by the Rhine)

legions.summary: Raised by Trajan c. 105 and numbered thirty because it brought the army to thirty legions. From c. 120 it held Vetera II beside Trajan's new colony at Xanten for three centuries.
legions.detail: It supported Septimius Severus in 193 and fought for him against Albinus in 197. Vexillations served in Mauretania and in the Parthian war of Severus. Under the Gallic emperors (260-274) it struck coin issues with its emblems.
scholarship: Ritterling, RE XII (1924-25) s.v. legio
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Le Bohec (ed.), Les légions de Rome sous le Haut-Empire (2000)
Bishop, Handbook to Roman Legionary Fortresses (2012)
